newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: IPO VIEW - LG Semicon's listing seen poorly timed.
newsitem.headline: IPO VIEW - LG Semicon's listing seen poorly timed.

text.p: Shares of LG Semicon, the world's seventh largest dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chip seller, will trade publicly for the first time on Saturday, but a dull market might cool its debut, analysts said on Thursday.

Not only are there questions of whether the market for semiconductors is improving, but a tidal wave of new issues, about 1.1 trillion won ($1.33 billion) worth, is waiting to swamp the Seoul bourse this month.
Earlier this week, the stock index fell to three-year lows. On Thursday, the market closed at 741.76, down nearly 25 percent from a year high of 986.84 in May.
The bourse has been hammered by an economic slowdown, the need to pay back record high loans for margin trading, an anti-corruption investigation, and oversupply fears.

"LG Semicon is a good company, with good technology which is rapidly advancing, but the timing of the issue is not so good," said Bruce Gonyea, regional technology analyst at Paribas Capital Markets in Singapore.
"There is a big crowd of investors who believe the cyclical upturn hasn't arrived yet."

According to securities house Hannuri-Salomon, the global oversupply of DRAM chips is seen lasting till 1997. It said prices could fall again later this year, when the market moves to third-generation chips and new capacity cranks up from Taiwan, South Korea and Japan.
Spot prices of 16-megabit DRAM chips have fallen about 80 percent to around $9 from a year earlier.
But some analysts said LG Semicon, a unit of the LG Group must list now because South Korean securities regulations require that a company must be profitable for three years before going public.

"I don't think this is a good time for Semicon to be listed because of the market sentiment, but I don't think the company has any other options," said Tony Jung, a Jardine Fleming Securities analyst in Seoul.
"Depending on the (DRAM) price level, the company might have a losing year, in terms of net profit. If that's the case, the company cannot be listed for another three years," he said.

"The timing of our listing has nothing to do with our performance. We've been trying to get listed since last year," said Kim Yong-sung, manager of LG Semicon's finance department, who denied that the company would face a loss next year.
"Timely investment is a requirement of the semiconductor industry. The listing is part of our efforts to raise funds for investment," he said.

Earnings forecasts for the LG Group unit varied widely. Due to the drop in DRAM prices, Jardine Fleming's Jung saw net profits in 1996 plummetting to 53 billion won on sales of 2.3 trillion won. Hannuri-Salomon put net profits at 165.3 billion on sales of 2.46 trillion.
For next year, Jardine Fleming forecast profits of 66 billion won on sales of 2.8 trillion won, while Hannuri-Salomon saw a swing to a loss of 92.1 billion on sales of 2.15 trillion.
LG Semicon posted a net profit of 779 billion won on sales of 2.5 trillion won last year.

The firm's 10 million new shares had a subscription price of 20,000 won per share at its initial public offering in September, and LG Semicon predicted the shares would rise to above 40,000 won when they went public.

But not everyone was so bullish. "I would buy the shares if they fell under 20,000 won," said Kevin Choi, a fund manager at Seoul Investment Trust Co. "I'd rather hold shares of Samsung Electronics, which is better positioned to benefit from an upturn in prices."

Jardine Fleming's Jung said he has recommended investors buy the shares up to the price of 25,000 won. "I think a lot of people think the cycle will be turning around, starting toward the end of next year," he said.

Including LG Semicon, initial offerings set for November are valued at about 450 billion won. Rights issues will inject about another 240 billion won, and 500 billion won of unlisted Korea Telecom shares will be auctioned by the government.
